title: Corporate Readiness and Interview Skills
tagline: From CV to offer to your first 90 days, with practice in every module
summary: Prepare for the world of work: find your direction, write a CV and cover letter, network, handle interviews and assessments, compare offers and start well. Every module has a hands-on lab.

modules.title: Career clarity
modules.summary: Know what you offer, what you want and what employers look for.
modules.outcome: You can list your proven skills, describe the kind of role you want and research an employer before applying.
modules.intro: Most people begin a job search by sending a CV to everything. A better way is to start with clarity: what can you prove you can do, what kind of work suits you and which employers value it?

topics.title: Skills, strengths and evidence
topics.html:
Definition

Evidence. A specific result or example that proves a claim. 'Good at teamwork' is a claim. 'Led a team of five to finish a project a week early' is evidence.

Three kinds of things you offer
KindMeaningExampleHow to show it
SkillsThings you can doWriting, spreadsheets, sellingExamples with results
StrengthsHow you naturally workCalm under pressure, curiousA short story
KnowledgeWhat you knowAccounting basics, a languageCourses, projects

Build your evidence list

  1. List ten things you have done in study, work, clubs or home projects.
  2. For each, write what you did and the result, with a number if possible.
  3. Underline the skills each one shows.
  4. Choose the five strongest and learn to tell them in two minutes.
Tip

Fresh graduates often think they have no experience. Projects, clubs, tutoring, family business and volunteering all count if you can show what you did and what happened.

When you list your evidence, include things that seem small. Organising a school trip, managing a shared budget, helping a neighbour set up a phone or running a study group all show initiative, planning and communication. Employers do not need grand stories; they need credible ones. A small story told precisely is far more convincing than a big claim told vaguely.

Check what you just learned

1. Which is evidence?
  • Hard-working
  • Raised 25,000 rupees for charity in a week (correct)
  • Team player
  • Good attitude

It is specific and measurable.
keyPoints: Back every claim with an example and a result.
Projects, clubs and volunteering count as experience.

topics.title: Choosing a direction
topics.html:
You do not need a lifelong plan. You need a next step that fits your skills, interests and the real jobs available. A useful check uses four questions.

Four questions
QuestionWhy it matters
What am I good at?Your skills and strengths
What do I enjoy?Motivation lasts longer than pay alone
What does the market pay for?Roles exist and are hiring
What suits my life now?Location, hours, money, learning
Worked example

From interests to roles

A student who likes organising events, writing and social media.

  1. Roles to explore: marketing assistant, events coordinator, content writer.
  2. Check job adverts: which skills do they ask for?
  3. Compare with your evidence list and close the gaps with small projects.

Answer. Real adverts tell you what employers want, so use them as your guide.

Research a role

  • Read ten job adverts and note repeated skills.
  • Talk to two people who do the job.
  • Search for typical pay for your location.
  • Find out how people usually enter the field.
Watch out

Be careful with offers that ask you to pay money before starting a job or to share bank passwords. Genuine employers do not charge candidates.

Check what you just learned

1. A fake job offer often asks you to:
  • Send a CV
  • Attend an interview
  • Pay a fee before starting (correct)
  • Share your skills

Genuine employers do not charge candidates.
keyPoints: Choose a next step using skills, interests, market demand and life situation.
Read real job adverts to learn what employers want.

topics.title: Researching employers
topics.html:
Before you apply

  1. Read the company's website: products, customers, values.
  2. Read recent news or posts: what are they proud of?
  3. Understand the job advert: what are the top three requirements?
  4. Find the hiring manager's name, if possible.
  5. Check reviews from current and former staff, with sensible caution.
What to note
ItemUse it in
Company missionCover letter, 'why us' answer
Recent achievementA compliment or a question
Required skillsYour CV keywords and stories
Culture hintsYour questions and tone

Common mistakes

  • Applying with the same CV and letter for every job.
  • Knowing nothing about the employer when asked 'Why us?'.
  • Trusting a single unverified review.
Tip

Prepare a one-sentence 'Why this company' that mentions something specific. It is one of the most common interview questions.

Check what you just learned

1. A good 'why us' answer is:
  • Because I need a job
  • Because you pay well
  • Because it is near home
  • Specific to the company's work (correct)

Specifics show genuine interest.

Key terms: flip and sort

Evidence
A specific result that proves a claim
Skill
Something you can do
Strength
How you work naturally
Job advert
A description of a vacancy
keyPoints: Research the company, the role and the people.
Prepare a specific 'why us'.

modules.title: CV and online profile
modules.summary: Build a CV and an online profile that get read.
modules.outcome: You can write achievement-based CV lines, structure a one-page CV and keep a professional online profile.
modules.intro: A CV has one job: to get you an interview. Recruiters look at a CV for seconds, so structure, evidence and clarity matter more than design.

topics.title: Structure of a one-page CV
topics.html:
Standard sections
SectionContent
Name and contactName, phone, email, city, link to your profile
SummaryTwo or three lines: who you are, what you offer, what you want
ExperienceMost recent first; achievements, not duties
SkillsRelevant skills and tools
EducationCourse, institution, year, notable project
ExtrasLanguages, volunteering, awards (only if relevant)

Layout rules

  • One page for a fresh graduate; two at most later.
  • Simple fonts, clear headings and consistent dates.
  • No photo, age or family details unless the country's custom requires it.
  • Save as PDF with a clear file name: Arjun-Rao-CV.pdf.
  • Proofread twice; a typo can lose an interview.
Tip

Use the same words as the job advert where they are true. Many companies use software that scans for keywords.

Ask a friend to look at your CV for ten seconds and then tell you what they remember. If they cannot name your strongest achievement, move it higher on the page or shorten the lines around it.

A good summary does three things in two or three lines: it states your field, gives your strongest proof, and says what you want next. For example: 'Marketing graduate who grew a student campaign by 40% and enjoys turning data into stories. Seeking a junior marketing role in food or consumer brands.' Avoid empty adjectives such as hard-working and passionate; show them through the lines that follow.

Check what you just learned

1. A fresh graduate's CV should usually be:
  • One page (correct)
  • Five pages
  • Ten pages
  • A video

Short is read.
keyPoints: One page: summary, experience, skills, education.
Use clear headings and keywords from the advert.

topics.title: Achievements, not duties
topics.html:
Formula · A strong line

Action verb + what you did + result (with a number)

Increased newsletter sign-ups by 35% by redesigning the form.

From duty to achievement
Duty (weak)Achievement (strong)
Responsible for social mediaGrew followers from 800 to 3,200 in two months
Helped customersResolved 30 customer queries a day with 95% satisfaction
Did data entryEntered and checked 1,200 records a week with no errors
Member of the clubOrganised three events for 150 members

Action verbs

  • Led, managed, organised, coordinated
  • Created, designed, wrote, built, launched
  • Improved, increased, reduced, saved, grew
  • Analysed, tested, evaluated, researched

Common mistakes

  • Writing 'responsible for' again and again.
  • Giving no numbers.
  • Exaggerating: be ready to explain every line in an interview.
Watch out

Never lie on a CV. False qualifications and dates are checked, and they can end an offer or a career later.

Check what you just learned

1. Which line is strongest?
  • Responsible for events
  • Organised three events for 150 members (correct)
  • Helped at events
  • Did events

It has action and numbers.
keyPoints: Use action verb, task and result with a number.
Be truthful and ready to explain each line.

topics.title: Your online profile
topics.html:
Employers search for candidates online. A short, professional profile helps; careless public posts can hurt. Think of it as a second CV.

A professional profile

  • A clear, friendly photo with a plain background.
  • A headline that states what you do and want, not just 'student'.
  • A summary in your own words, with two or three proofs.
  • Experience and projects with results.
  • Skills and a few genuine recommendations.
  • Privacy settings checked on personal accounts.
Search yourself
CheckAction
Search your nameSee what an employer sees
Old public postsDelete or hide anything you would not say at an interview
Email addressUse a plain professional one
Profile linksPut the best one on your CV
Tip

Update your profile whenever you finish a project or a course, while the details are fresh.

Check what you just learned

1. Before applying you should:
  • Hide your email
  • Delete your CV
  • Search your own name online (correct)
  • Avoid all profiles

Employers do.

Key terms: flip and sort

CV
A document summarising your work and skills
Summary
The short introduction at the top of a CV
Action verb
A strong verb that begins a line
Keyword
A term an employer or software looks for
keyPoints: Treat your online profile as a second CV.
Search your own name and tidy what you find.

modules.title: Cover letters and networking
modules.summary: Write letters that connect you to the job, and build useful relationships honestly.
modules.outcome: You can write a short cover letter, find and approach people in your field and follow up politely.
modules.intro: Most jobs are found through people as much as adverts. A good letter and a respectful message can open doors that a CV alone cannot.

topics.title: The cover letter
topics.html:
Weak and strong openings
WeakStrong
I am writing to apply for the post advertised.I am applying for the junior marketing role at Greenleaf Foods, where I can use my experience of growing a student campaign by 40%.

Rules

  1. Address a person where you can.
  2. One page, three to four short paragraphs.
  3. Do not repeat the CV; add the story behind a key line.
  4. Match the tone of the company.
  5. Proofread the company name and the role.

Common mistakes

  • Copying the same letter to every company and forgetting to change the name.
  • Starting with 'I am a hard-working person'.
  • Asking for sympathy instead of showing value.

Check what you just learned

1. A cover letter should mainly:
  • Repeat the CV
  • List hobbies
  • Tell your life story
  • Connect your best proof to their need (correct)

It adds the story behind the CV.
keyPoints: Four paragraphs: why, proof, why them, next step.
Never send a generic letter.

topics.title: Networking that works
topics.html:
Networking is not collecting contacts; it is building honest relationships by being curious and useful. A short, specific request is easier to accept than a vague 'please give me a job'.

A good message
PartExample
Who you areI am a final-year commerce student
Why themI read your talk on healthy-food campaigns
A small askCould I have 15 minutes to learn how you started?
FlexibilityI can fit any time that suits you
ThanksThank you for considering this

Where to meet people

  • Alumni of your college.
  • Industry events and webinars.
  • Professional groups online.
  • Former teachers and club leaders.
  • Friends and family who know people at work.
Tip

After a conversation, send a thank-you within a day and tell the person what you did with their advice. People help those who follow through.

Watch out

Never ask a stranger for a job in your first message, and never send mass identical messages. Be specific and respectful of their time.

Check what you just learned

1. A good first networking ask is:
  • 15 minutes of advice (correct)
  • A job offer
  • Money
  • A referral for anything

A small ask is easy to accept.
keyPoints: Ask for advice and a small amount of time, not a job.
Thank people and follow up.

topics.title: Applying and following up
topics.html:
Track your applications
ColumnWhy
Company and roleRemember what you applied for
Date appliedPlan follow-ups
ContactWho to write to
StatusApplied, interview, offer, declined
NotesWhat to improve next time

Follow-up etiquette

  • Wait at least one week unless a date was given.
  • Keep it short and polite.
  • Reattach nothing unless asked; restate your interest in one line.
  • Accept silence gracefully: many employers cannot reply to everyone.

Common mistakes

  • Applying to a hundred jobs with one version of the CV.
  • Not recording what you sent.
  • Sending angry messages after a rejection.

Check what you just learned

1. After applying, a polite follow-up usually comes:
  • The same day
  • After about a week (correct)
  • Every hour
  • Never

Give time.

Key terms: flip and sort

Cover letter
A letter linking you to a job
Network
People who know and help each other
Follow-up
A polite reminder
Referral
A recommendation from an insider
keyPoints: Tailor each application and track it.
Follow up once, politely.

modules.title: Interviews
modules.summary: Prepare stories, answer common questions and handle different interview formats with calm.
modules.outcome: You can answer common questions with the STAR method, prepare strong questions and perform well on video and in person.
modules.intro: An interview tests three things: can you do the job, will you fit, and do you want it. Preparation is the single biggest factor under your control.

topics.title: The STAR method
topics.html:
Worked example

A STAR answer

Question: Tell me about a time you worked under pressure.

  1. Situation: Our college fest had two weeks left and only 40% of tickets sold.
  2. Task: I led promotion and had to double daily sales.
  3. Action: I created a referral offer, asked each class representative to share it and posted daily videos.
  4. Result: We sold out three days early and the referral offer brought 40% of all sales.

Answer. A short story with a measured result is far more convincing than saying 'I work well under pressure'.

Tips

  • Prepare five stories that can answer many questions: teamwork, challenge, leadership, failure, initiative.
  • Keep each under two minutes.
  • Use I for your own actions and we for the team's result.
  • End with what you learned.
Tip

Practise aloud. Reading your answer in your head hides the gaps.

Check what you just learned

1. In STAR, the 'A' should describe:
  • What the team felt
  • The company history
  • What you personally did (correct)
  • Your plans

The interviewer wants your contribution.
keyPoints: Situation, Task, Action, Result.
Prepare five reusable stories.

topics.title: Common questions
topics.html:
Frequent questions and what they test
QuestionWhat they want to knowHow to answer
Tell me about yourselfCan you summarise yourself relevantly?A 60-second pitch: present, past, future, linked to the role
Why this company?Did you research? Do you care?Something specific you admire
Your strengths?Are they relevant and honest?Two strengths with examples
Your weakness?Self-awarenessA real, minor weakness and what you are doing about it
Why should we hire you?Fit and valueSummarise your top proof and how it helps them
Where do you see yourself in five years?Ambition and fitGrowth in the field, not a specific title
Watch out

Do not criticise former employers, teachers or teams. Describe challenges neutrally and focus on what you learned.

Common mistakes

  • Memorising scripts that sound robotic.
  • Giving one-word answers.
  • Rambling for five minutes.
  • Saying your weakness is 'working too hard'.

A pitch of about sixty seconds helps with the most common opener. Structure it in three parts: present (what you do now), past (the experience that prepared you) and future (why this role). Practise until it sounds natural, and adapt it to each interview.

Check what you just learned

1. A good answer about weakness is:
  • I have none
  • I am perfect
  • I work too hard
  • A real minor weakness and how I am improving it (correct)

It shows self-awareness.
keyPoints: Prepare a 60-second pitch and honest answers for the usual questions.
Never criticise others.

topics.title: Formats, nerves and etiquette
topics.html:
Interview formats
FormatTips
PhoneQuiet room, stand up to sound energetic, have notes ready
VideoTest the camera and sound, plain background, look at the camera, dress as for in person
PanelAddress everyone; make eye contact with the person asking
Group exerciseListen, build on others' ideas and keep to time
Case or technicalThink aloud and structure your answer

Before the day

  1. Check the route or link and arrive ten minutes early.
  2. Bring copies of your CV and a notebook.
  3. Dress one level smarter than the daily job.
  4. Sleep well; do not memorise at midnight.

Handling nerves

  • Breathe slowly through the nose for a minute.
  • Use a short pause before answering.
  • Remember the interviewers want you to succeed.
  • It is fine to say, 'Let me think for a moment'.
Tip

Send a short thank-you email the same day, mentioning one thing you enjoyed learning in the conversation.

Check what you just learned

1. After an interview you should:
  • Send a short thank-you (correct)
  • Say nothing
  • Ask about pay again
  • Criticise

Courtesy stays in memory.

Key terms: flip and sort

STAR
Situation, task, action, result
Panel interview
Several interviewers at once
Behavioural question
A question about past behaviour
Pitch
A short self-introduction
keyPoints: Prepare for the format: phone, video, panel, case.
Arrive early, breathe, and send a thank-you.

modules.title: Assessments, offers and negotiation
modules.summary: Handle tests and group tasks, compare offers fairly and negotiate respectfully.
modules.outcome: You can prepare for assessments, compare offers by total value and negotiate with evidence.
modules.intro: Selection is often more than an interview: tests, group tasks and background checks. Then comes the offer and the question of money. Treat both with preparation.

topics.title: Tests and group exercises
topics.html:
Common assessments
TypeWhat is testedHow to prepare
Aptitude or logicReasoning and numeracyPractise sample questions under time
Skills testJob-specific tasks (writing, spreadsheet, code)Review fundamentals and do mock tasks
Group exerciseTeamwork and leadershipListen, include quiet members, summarise
PresentationStructure and deliveryPractise aloud with a timer
Case studyStructured thinkingFrame the problem, list options, recommend

In a group exercise

  • Do not dominate or hide.
  • Build on others' points by name.
  • Keep time and summarise.
  • Disagree respectfully and offer reasons.
  • Help the group reach a decision.
Tip

In a timed test, answer the easy questions first and mark the hard ones to return to.

Check what you just learned

1. In a group exercise a good habit is:
  • Interrupting
  • Summarising and including others (correct)
  • Staying silent
  • Taking over

Collaboration is assessed.
keyPoints: Practise sample tests; behave as a good teammate in groups.
Manage time in tests.

topics.title: Understanding an offer
topics.html:
An offer is more than the headline salary. Compare the whole package and the costs of getting to work.

Parts of a package
PartQuestions
Base salaryFixed monthly or yearly pay
Variable pay or bonusHow is it calculated and how often is it actually paid?
BenefitsInsurance, leave, retirement contributions
LearningTraining budget, mentoring
CostsCommute, relocation, equipment
TermsProbation, notice period, working hours, place
Formula · Net yearly value

net = total package value - yearly costs of working

Compare offers on net value, then add the less measurable factors: growth, people, stability.

Compare two packages

Change the numbers to see how commuting and bonuses change the net value.

Adjust Base salary (yearly rupees), Bonus and benefits (yearly rupees), Daily commute cost (rupees), Working days per year and see Total package, Yearly commute cost, Net yearly value change.

Watch out

Read the offer letter carefully. Ask for anything verbal to be written down before you accept.

Check what you just learned

1. Which should be part of comparing offers?
  • Only the base salary
  • The company logo
  • Total package and costs (correct)
  • The office colour

Net value matters.
keyPoints: Compare total package minus costs.
Get the terms in writing.

topics.title: Negotiating respectfully
topics.html:
What to say
SituationSentence
OpeningThank you, I am excited about the role.
EvidenceBased on my research and my project results, I was hoping for a base of X.
AlternativesIf the salary is fixed, could we look at training budget or review in six months?
ClosingThank you; could you send the updated offer in writing?

Principles

  1. Research typical pay for the role, location and experience.
  2. Know your minimum and your ideal.
  3. Negotiate once, calmly, with reasons.
  4. Think about the whole package.
  5. Accept or decline politely within the agreed time.

Common mistakes

  • Accepting at once without reading.
  • Making demands or threats.
  • Lying about other offers.
  • Negotiating by text message in anger.

Check what you just learned

1. During negotiation you should:
  • Lie about other offers
  • Hide
  • Threaten
  • Use research and stay calm (correct)

Evidence and courtesy work.

Key terms: flip and sort

Package
All pay and benefits together
Probation
An initial trial period
Notice period
Time to give before leaving a job
Net value
Total minus the costs of working
keyPoints: Research, ask once with reasons and consider the whole package.
Be honest and get changes in writing.

steps: Add the total package for each.
Subtract the yearly costs.

Make a decision and explain why.

modules.title: Your first 90 days
modules.summary: Start well, build trust and keep growing.
modules.outcome: You can plan your first three months, ask for feedback and handle early challenges professionally.
modules.intro: The first weeks of a job shape how people see you for years. A simple plan, curiosity and reliability matter more than showing off.

topics.title: A 30-60-90 day plan
topics.html:
The three phases
PhaseFocusTypical actions
First 30 daysLearnMeet people, understand customers, products and processes, agree what success looks like
Days 31 to 60ContributeOwn small tasks, deliver them well, ask for feedback often
Days 61 to 90ImproveSuggest improvements with evidence, take on a project, set goals for the next quarter

Habits that build trust

  • Be on time and do what you say.
  • Write things down; do not ask the same question twice.
  • Ask for help early, with what you tried.
  • Say thank you and credit others.
  • Tell your manager about problems early.
Tip

In your first week ask your manager: 'What would make you say in three months that I was a great hire?' Then plan backwards.

Check what you just learned

1. The first 30 days are mostly for:
  • Learning (correct)
  • Quitting
  • Changing everything
  • Resting

Understand before you change.
keyPoints: Learn, contribute, then improve.
Reliability and early honesty build trust.

topics.title: Feedback and growth
topics.html:
Feedback is information, not a verdict. People who ask for it regularly improve faster and are trusted more.

Asking for feedback
Instead ofAsk
Am I doing OK?What is one thing I could do better in how I present reports?
SilenceCould we have ten minutes every two weeks to review my progress?

When you receive feedback

  1. Listen without defending.
  2. Thank the person.
  3. Ask for an example if unclear.
  4. Decide what you will do and tell them.
  5. Follow up later to show progress.

Common mistakes

  • Taking criticism as a personal attack.
  • Not asking until the review meeting.
  • Promising change and doing nothing.

Check what you just learned

1. Receiving feedback well means:
  • Defending yourself at once
  • Listening and thanking (correct)
  • Arguing
  • Ignoring

Show you can grow.
keyPoints: Ask for specific feedback regularly.
Thank, act and follow up.

topics.title: Professional conduct and wellbeing
topics.html:
Professional habits

  • Respect confidentiality: do not share company information.
  • Use company tools and time properly.
  • Keep personal social posts free of complaints about colleagues.
  • Take breaks and protect your sleep.
  • Speak up about safety or unfair treatment through the right channels.
Handling common early challenges
ChallengeResponse
Unclear tasksAsk the purpose, deadline and format
Too much workShow your list and ask which to prioritise
Conflict with a colleagueTalk privately and calmly using facts; ask for help if it persists
MistakesReport quickly, fix, learn
Watch out

If you face harassment, discrimination or unsafe conditions, do not stay silent. Use your company's procedure and, where needed, local authorities or support organisations.

Tip

Keep a short weekly list of what you achieved. It makes reviews, CV updates and promotion discussions easy.

Check what you just learned

1. When you make a mistake, the best move is to:
  • Hide it
  • Blame others
  • Report it quickly and fix it (correct)
  • Quit

Honesty builds trust.

Key terms: flip and sort

30-60-90 plan
A three-phase start-up plan
Probation
A trial period
Feedback
Information about your performance
Confidentiality
Keeping company information private
keyPoints: Be reliable, confidential and kind; speak up when something is wrong.
Keep a record of your achievements.

List who you will ask for feedback.
